To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have demonstrated that the Swift satellite can be used for rapid follow up observations of gravitational wave candidate events and that we have shown the sensitivity improvement joint GW and electromagnetic observations could bring in the future.
we performed the first multi wavelength observations of two candidate GW transient events and that we demonstrated the feasibility of rapid GW transient follow up.
We have demonstrated that a joint electromagnetic and GW observation program is technically feasible.
In summary, our research is concerned with
gravitational waves (GW) and their sources.
the identification of the progenitors of compact binary inspiral GW sources.

the development of the observational infrastructure for electromagnetic follow up of GW transients with a special emphasis on those joint observations capable of completing the identification of the GW source.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have shown that we are capable of performing follow up observations of GW candidates in the time scales of minutes, with a telescope of 1 m class.

the data presented here are fully consistent with the hypothesis that GW transients of the types described here are of an astrophysically natural origin, and do not contain a significant component of non astrophysical signals.

the first multi wavelength GW follow up observations are successful in demonstrating the feasibility of the approach and that the sensitivity of the combined search for GW transients and their counterparts is better than for each individual one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

this was a successful test and demonstration of the feasibility of multi wavelength follow up for routine GW transients and that we are now ready for routine observations in the advanced GW detector era.

we have demonstrated that the combined use of LIGO, Virgo, and Swift is a promising method for identifying GW sources, but we need a larger sample of GW transients before reaching a firm conclusion on its sensitivity.
the non detection of electromagnetic transients is consistent with the LIGO-Virgo upper limits on the GW emission computed from the candidate events.
The main takeaway from our work is that
with the advanced detectors we will be able to perform significant source localization, which will open a new era in multi wavelength follow up.

rapid multi wavelength follow ups of GW candidates, together with a rapid off line analysis of the data, can help determine the statistical significance of the GW transients and hence reduce the contribution of false events to the astrophysical sample.

with the present instruments we could be testing GW sources within a few hundred megaparsecs, and the advanced instruments will be able to probe the nearby Universe and detect binary coalescences within our own Galaxy.
